network.overall_strategy: To achieve prebiotic L-alanine synthesis, the network employs a diverse, environment-rationalized approach rooted in experimentally supported and chemically plausible routes. The main strategies combine Strecker-type aminonitrile formation/hydrolysis, transamination from α-ketoacids, reductive amination of pyruvate, formaldehyde–acetaldehyde C–C coupling, and UV/thermal aldehyde chemistry, using intermediates such as HCN, ammonia, pyruvate, acetaldehyde, and methylamine. All reactions are explicitly atom- and charge-balanced; water and byproducts are included where required. Multiple environmental contexts are utilized, from mineral-catalyzed hydrothermal synthesis to surface photochemistry and prebiotic pools, deliberately mapping interconnected alternative entry points for the synthesis of L-alanine. Ten chemically robust pathways are formulated, each fully specifying molecules, balanced reactions, justified minerals/catalysts, and appropriate geochemical logic.

reactions.name: Methane and ammonia to hydrogen cyanide
reactions.mechanism: Partial oxidation of methane and ammonia on FeS/FeNiS surfaces generates HCN and water.
reactions.reasoning: Hydrothermal FeS-catalyzed methane + ammonia partial oxidation is a recognized source of steady-state HCN (Brandes et al., 1998; McCollom, 2013).

reactions.name: Formaldehyde formation from CO2 reduction

conditions.other: Reductive, possibly driven by H2/metal redox couples

reactions.mechanism: CO2 is stepwise reduced to formaldehyde on iron-nickel sulfide interfaces.
reactions.reasoning: CO2 reduction to C1s under hydrothermal conditions is widely supported (Cody et al., 2000; Herschy et al., 2014).

reactions.name: Acetaldehyde synthesis by aldol condensation of formaldehyde and methane derivatives

conditions.other: UV irradiation, partial dehydration at air–water interface

reactions.mechanism: Formaldehyde undergoes condensation with methyl radicals from photolyzed methane to form acetaldehyde.
reactions.reasoning: Surface aldehyde formation by UV/macromolecular catalysis is established (Sita et al., 1972; Saladino et al., 2012).

reactions.name: Pyruvate formation from acetaldehyde oxidation and CO2 addition
reactions.mechanism: Acetaldehyde reacts with CO2 and water on FeS to afford pyruvate via carboxylation/oxidation.
reactions.reasoning: Prebiotic pyruvate synthesis from simple aldehydes and CO2 is supported (Huber & Wächtershäuser, 1997; Muchowska et al., 2017).

reactions.name: Pyruvate reductive amination to alanine
reactions.mechanism: Reductive amination of pyruvate yields L-alanine and water.
reactions.reasoning: Reductive amination of α-ketoacids is the principal biochemical route; surface/mineral or UV-catalyzed amination is plausible prebiotically (Raiswell et al., 2002; Weber, 1984).

reactions.name: Strecker synthesis of alanine aminonitrile

conditions.other: Mildly alkaline evaporitic pool, wet-dry cycling

reactions.mechanism: Acetaldehyde, ammonia, and HCN react by Strecker synthesis to form alanine aminonitrile plus water.
reactions.reasoning: Strecker reactions for α-amino acids are strongly supported (Lazcano & Bada, 2004; Pizzarello et al., 2006).

reactions.name: Hydrolysis of alanine aminonitrile to L-alanine
reactions.mechanism: Alanine aminonitrile is hydrolyzed to L-alanine.
reactions.reasoning: Geochemical and experimental precedents for clay-catalyzed aminonitrile hydrolysis (Barge et al., 2017; Saladino et al., 2001).

reactions.name: Acetonitrile hydrolysis to amide then to methylamine
reactions.mechanism: Stepwise hydration of acetonitrile forms methylamine.
reactions.reasoning: Methylamine is a recognized product of acetonitrile hydrolysis on clays (Peltzer & Bada, 1978).

reactions.name: Methylamine to L-alanine via formose–transamination sequence
reactions.mechanism: Methylamine reacts with formaldehyde and ammonia, yielding imine intermediates that hydrolyze to L-alanine.
reactions.reasoning: Imine chemistry with methylamines and C1s supports α-amino acid formation—even without specific catalysts (Weber, 1998).

reactions.name: Reductive amination of acetic acid to alanine
reactions.mechanism: Acetic acid, NH3, and formaldehyde undergo condensation and amination to yield alanine and water.
reactions.reasoning: Similar reactions with C2/C1s and ammonia give α-amino acids, especially on FeS (Huber & Wächtershäuser, 1998; speculative for pure acetic–formaldehyde but logical extension).

reactions.name: HCN trimerization and hydrolysis to acetonitrile
reactions.mechanism: HCN is photochemically trimerized; partial hydrolysis gives acetonitrile.
reactions.reasoning: HCN-derived species, including acetonitrile, are observed in irradiated evaporites (Ferris et al., 1978; Ferus et al., 2017).

reactions.name: Lactonitrile (2-hydroxypropanenitrile) formation from acetaldehyde and HCN
reactions.mechanism: HCN addition to acetaldehyde produces lactonitrile.
reactions.reasoning: Condensation of HCN to aldehydes is well documented, borates enhance intermediate stability (Ricardo et al., 2004).

reactions.name: Hydrolysis of lactonitrile to alanine
reactions.mechanism: Lactonitrile hydrolyzed by ammonia and water yields alanine.
reactions.reasoning: Aminonitrile and hydroxy nitrile hydrolysis to amino acids is robust on clays (Saladino et al., 2001; Pizzarello et al., 2006).

reactions.name: Aldol addition, imine, and Strecker-like conversion to 2-aminopropanal
reactions.mechanism: Aldol addition of acetaldehyde/formaldehyde with imine formation and rearrangement yields 2-aminopropanal.
reactions.reasoning: Imine/aldol network chemistry of aldehydes/amines is extensively supported (Weber, 1998).

reactions.name: Aminopropanal hydrolysis to alanine
reactions.reasoning: Stabilized intermediates from imine/aldol reactions hydrolyze to α-amino acids (Barge et al., 2017).

reactions.name: 2-aminopropanol oxidation to alanine

conditions.other: Oxidation via mineral catalysts or photolysis

reactions.reasoning: Amino alcohols are plausible precursors; oxidation by UV/FeS supports α-amino acid formation (Wang et al., 2019; speculative for prebiotic catalysis).

reactions.name: 2-hydroxypropanenitrile (lactonitrile) reductive amination to 2-aminopropanol
reactions.mechanism: Reductive amination of α-hydroxynitriles affords amino alcohols.
reactions.reasoning: Reductive amination mechanisms are described for related systems; speculation, but logical (Weber, 1984).

reactions.name: Acetic acid formation from acetaldehyde oxidation
reactions.mechanism: Acetaldehyde oxidized to acetic acid on FeS surface.
reactions.reasoning: Such conversions are well-known on FeS and related minerals under hydrothermal vent conditions (Huber & Wächtershäuser, 1997).

pathways.name: Hydrothermal–reductive amination pathway via pyruvate
pathways.description: Starts with CO2 → formaldehyde → acetaldehyde → pyruvate in hydrothermal settings, completed by reductive amination to L-alanine.

pathways.name: Strecker route from acetaldehyde
pathways.description: Classic Strecker pathway using acetaldehyde, ammonia, and HCN yielding aminonitrile then hydrolyzing to L-alanine.

pathways.name: Acetonitrile–methylamine–formaldehyde transamination route
pathways.description: HCN from hydrothermal, trimerized to acetonitrile, hydrolyzed to methylamine, then condensed with formaldehyde and ammonia to L-alanine.

pathways.name: Acetic acid plus ammonia/formaldehyde reductive amination
pathways.description: Acetaldehyde from formaldehyde/methane yields acetic acid (hydrothermal), which condenses with ammonia and formaldehyde to form L-alanine.

pathways.name: Lactonitrile (2-hydroxypropanenitrile) route
pathways.description: Acetaldehyde and HCN form lactonitrile, hydrolyzed directly to L-alanine.

pathways.name: Aldol/imine route via aminopropanal
pathways.description: Acetaldehyde, ammonia, and formaldehyde undergo condensation yielding aminopropanal, which is hydrolyzed to L-alanine.

pathways.name: Methylamine–formaldehyde–ammonia one-pot formation
pathways.description: Methylamine (from acetaldehyde/acetonitrile route) reacts directly with formaldehyde and ammonia, forming L-alanine in a one-pot imine-driven process.

pathways.name: HCN–formaldehyde–methylamine three-component route
pathways.description: HCN (hydrothermal) and formaldehyde yield key C2/C3 intermediates, which after ammonia/methylamine-driven transformations give L-alanine.

pathways.name: Lactonitrile reduction–oxidation sequence (lactonitrile via aminopropanol)
pathways.description: Lactonitrile is aminated to 2-aminopropanol then oxidized to L-alanine.

pathways.name: Pyruvate formation from acetic acid and CO2, then amination
pathways.description: Acetaldehyde is oxidized to acetic acid (hydrothermal), then carboxylated to pyruvate, which is aminated to L-alanine.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Multiple key steps (CO2/water to formaldehyde, acetaldehyde to pyruvate, and pyruvate amination) are not mass-balanced as written, indicating conservation violations and possible missing species or misassigned stoichiometry. Environmental progression (hydrothermal/biochemical) is plausible, but these balance/feasibility issues undermine the route.
suggestions: Balance all reactions atomically; ensure all byproducts (like H2, O2, CO, or CO2) are included.
Adjust stoichiometry, especially in redox transformations.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The Strecker pathway is largely plausible, but the hydrolysis of alanine aminonitrile (rxn_007) is unbalanced (missing NH3). rxn_003 (formaldehyde-based acetaldehyde formation) is balanceable. The main issue is the atomic conservation in rxn_007; otherwise, chemistry and environmental logic are sound.
suggestions: Include all expected byproducts such as ammonia in aminonitrile hydrolysis.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Key reactions (HCN to acetonitrile, acetonitrile hydrolysis to methylamine, amination to alanine) are not balanced or involve formula inconsistencies. Methylamine route is interesting but not viable without resolving significant element conservation errors.
suggestions: Clarify all formulae; fix atom counts in the methylamine formation steps.
Break down multi-step conversions more clearly.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Reductive amination of acetic acid is chemically plausible but step rxn_018 (acetaldehyde oxidation) is not balanced. Reaction mechanisms in this sequence are otherwise feasible, and environments are appropriate.
suggestions: Balance oxidation steps and account for all protons/electrons/byproducts.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Lactonitrile formation is plausible and well-balanced, but the hydrolysis to alanine again misses an ammonia byproduct. The last step is neither atomically nor nitrogen balanced, which weakens the chemical soundness.
suggestions: Ensure full balancing of hydrolysis steps including all nitrogen sources and sinks.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Aminopropanal hydrolysis (rxn_015) is not balanced; other steps are plausible and fit surface chemistry. Pathway is appealing but needs proper mass/charge conservation details.
suggestions: Write all reactions with explicit balance; check H2 or NH3 as byproduct.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Problems with acetonitrile to methylamine conversion and methylamine/formaldehyde chemistry: not mass/charge balanced, and some steps possibly misassigned. Not currently viable.
suggestions: Expand on methylamine/redox conversion; check all atom counts.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: HCN-based methylamine route is inconsistent with balanced chemistry and omits intermediate byproducts. Stoichiometry needs careful revision.
suggestions: Explore alternative HCN functionalization or verify step-by-step carbon/nitrogen flow.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Several steps (2-hydroxypropanenitrile to aminopropanol, and then to alanine) are not mass balanced (missing C, O, N), and possible formula inconsistencies are noted for these intermediates. Needs revision.
suggestions: Clarify structures/InChI for aminopropanol; specify all byproducts.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Acetic acid and CO2 to pyruvate is not mass balanced, and downstream amination conserves neither hydrogen nor carbon without further species. Otherwise, the environmental steps are rational.
suggestions: Explicitly add all expected byproducts for carboxylation and reductive amination steps.

evaluation.network_feedback: The network creatively assembles a range of plausible prebiotic routes to L-alanine, drawing on robust chemical space and multiple environments. However, omissions of byproducts, widespread mass and charge conservation violations (especially for pyruvate, Strecker, ammonolysis, and methylamine pathways), and some possible formula inconsistencies (notably in aminopropanol/aminonitrile steps) undermine feasibility across nearly all paths. Chemical soundness could be restored by careful stoichiometric re-writing of affected reactions, inclusion of all minor byproducts, and explicitly checking the consistency of molecular formulae. Only the Strecker-type path (P2) approaches approval, pending resolution of hydrolysis byproducts. Literature and environmental logic are strong, but the network as written cannot currently be approved due to pervasive mass balance errors.
